one_liner: Small C++ header-only W-TinyLFU cache: frequency-sketch admission in front of segmented LRU, for higher hit ratios than plain LRU.
what_it_does: An in-process key/value cache template, wtinylfu_cache<K, V>, bounded by entry count. It replaces plain LRU eviction with the W-TinyLFU policy from the TinyLFU paper so that frequently used items survive scans and one-hit-wonder traffic. The API is small: get(key) or operator[] return std::shared_ptr<V> (nullptr on a miss), plus insert(key, value), get_and_insert_if_missing(key, loader), erase, contains, change_capacity and hit/miss counters. There is no iteration, TTL, weighting, byte-size bound or eviction callback.
how_it_is_fast: The gain is in hit ratio, not per-operation speed. A count-min sketch of 4-bit counters (four counters per key, packed sixteen to a 64-bit word, following Caffeine) estimates each key's recent frequency. Once about 10x capacity increments have been recorded, every counter is halved (the paper's 'reset' aging). New keys go into an LRU window sized at 1% of capacity. The window's LRU victim is admitted into a 99% segmented LRU (80% protected, 20% probationary) only if its estimated frequency is strictly higher than that of the probationary segment's LRU victim; otherwise the newcomer is dropped. Each get() pays a std::map lookup, a std::list splice, four sketch increments and a shared_ptr copy, so it costs more per call than a hand-rolled LRU. A Bloom-filter 'doorkeeper' header ships in the repo but is not wired in.
when_to_use: Single-threaded, or externally locked, in-process C++ object caches where plain LRU loses hit ratio to scans or to skewed (Zipf-like) traffic full of one-time keys.
Keys that are integers or padding-free POD ids. The sketch hashes the key's raw bytes, so only these keys hash consistently.

Expensive or large values (the repo's test caches 4 KB objects), where each extra hit is worth more than the policy's per-operation overhead (map lookup, list splice, sketch updates), and where returning shared_ptr keeps an evicted value alive while a caller still uses it.
As a readable reference (under 900 lines across four headers, including license text) to vendor and harden when you need W-TinyLFU in C++ and cannot use the JVM.
Frequency-skewed workloads like the paper's search-engine, DS1 and SPC1-like traces, where the fixed 1% window tied or beat LRU, ARC and LIRS.
when_not_to_use: Multithreaded access without your own lock. Even get() mutates the LRU order and the sketch, and a single global mutex serializes every operation.

Recency-heavy or 'sparse burst' workloads such as the paper's OLTP, F1 and F2 traces, which needed a 20-40% window. This port hard-codes a 1% window and an 80/20 split, with no hill-climbing adaptation of the kind Caffeine now does.
Untrusted or adversarial keys. There is no HashDoS protection: Caffeine's random admission of 'warm' candidates is missing, and issue #1 has been open since 2017.
std::string keys, or structs with pointers or padding. Equal keys hash differently, so admission decisions silently degrade.

Windows/MSVC builds, caches bounded by bytes or needing expiry, or latency-critical hot paths. Every insert does three heap allocations (std::map node, std::list node, make_shared block) and stores two copies of the key, and no throughput benchmark exists.

integration.min_toolchain: README says C++11, but detail.hpp's constexpr functions contain loops and multiple statements, which needs C++14 relaxed constexpr in practice. No compiler versions are documented and there is no CI.
integration.platforms: Portable C++ with no SIMD or intrinsics. It assumes a 64-bit long (LP64, e.g. Linux/macOS on x86-64 or aarch64): the sketch shifts 1L/0xfL by up to 60 bits, which is undefined where long is 32-bit (Windows).
integration.thread_safety: Not thread-safe. The header says 'NOTE: it is NOT thread-safe!', and get() mutates state, so every call needs an external lock. Returned shared_ptr<V> values stay valid after eviction. The circonus-labs fork (2023) adds a single global std::mutex.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it has the same get/insert/erase shape as a typical std::list + map LRU cache, but get returns std::shared_ptr<V> (nullptr on a miss), K needs operator< (the index is std::map, not a hash map) plus a byte-stable representation, and there are no custom hash, comparator or allocator parameters

gotchas: The sketch hashes the key's raw object bytes (Jenkins one-at-a-time over reinterpret_cast<const char*>(&key)), not std::hash. For std::string, or any key holding pointers or padding, the caller's key and the cache's stored copy can hash differently, so frequency comparisons turn into noise and nothing reports it.

Capacity edge cases (found by reading the code, not by running it): with capacity 1 the main SLRU gets 0 slots, and the second insert reads the victim of an empty probationary list, which is undefined behavior. Shrinking with change_capacity() can hit the same path when the protected segment holds more entries than the new capacity. change_capacity() also clears the sketch and, because is_full uses >=, evicts one entry more than needed.

insert() on an existing key only swaps the value. It does not refresh recency or bump the sketch; only get() records accesses. If the window is full it runs an eviction first anyway, so an update can shrink a full cache by one entry.

Portability: uint32_t, std::enable_if, std::max, std::min and std::hash are used without including <cstdint>, <type_traits>, <algorithm> or <functional>. The code relies on transitive includes of the kind GCC 13 removed from libstdc++. The hit and miss counters are plain int and overflow after 2^31.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: On the JVM, use Caffeine: it is the canonical W-TinyLFU, with an adaptive window, HashDoS jitter and concurrency. For offline trace studies, libCacheSim (SIEVE's repo) already ships WTinyLFU.c next to SIEVE, LRU and ARC. Pick this one only when you want a tiny dependency-free C++ W-TinyLFU object to embed in a single-threaded component with integer keys and are prepared to fix its edge cases. If you mainly need a simpler, better-than-LRU C++ policy, SIEVE or LHD have stronger evidence.
verified_claims_summary: This C++ port has no benchmark of its own. The only evidence is hit-ratio plots in the TinyLFU paper (arXiv 1512.00727v2), which the authors produced with a Java prototype and with Caffeine 2.0 on Zipf 0.7/0.94, SPC1-like and real traces. There, W-TinyLFU with a 1% window tied or beat LRU, ARC and LIRS on most traces, but OLTP, F1 and F2 needed a 20-40% window, which this port cannot configure. Hit ratio does not depend on hardware, and no compiler, hardware or throughput figures exist for this code.
status_note: Abandoned: the last commit was 2018-10-24, there are no releases, and six issues opened in 2017-2018 are still open, including HashDoS protection and 'Thorough testing required'. GitHub detects no license and there is no LICENSE file, but every header carries an MIT-style permission notice (Copyright 2017 mandreyel), so it is best treated as a small reference to vendor and fix rather than a dependency.
